title: Krishna Ella's Uneasy Return to Make a Cheap Hepatitis B Vaccine
dek: In 1996 a scientist in South Carolina sold up and moved to Hyderabad to make a hepatitis B vaccine that India's lenders doubted could be made cheaply.

story.event: Leaving a US research post in 1996 to found Bharat Biotech and make a low-cost hepatitis B vaccine
story.summary: In 1996 Krishna Ella left a research post at the Medical University of South Carolina and, with his wife Suchitra, sold their US assets and founded Bharat Biotech in Hyderabad to make a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine. After a promised venture investment stalled, the Industrial Development Bank of India took a stake, and the vaccine, Revac-B, reached the market in January 1999. By 2003 UNICEF was buying it at 23 cents a dose.
paragraphs: In 1996 Krishna Ella held a research post in pharmacology at the Medical University of South Carolina in Charleston, three years after finishing a PhD at the University of Wisconsin. He came from a farming family near Madras and had left a job with Bayer in India for the United States in 1986. Going home was not his idea. "I was not so comfortable about the idea," he said in 2000; his wife, Suchitra, insisted they do something in India where his science would be useful to ordinary people. Later he also credited his mother, recalling her words: "No matter how much you earn, you cannot eat more than this capacity."

He knew what he wanted to make. His speciality was gene expression in yeast, and he wanted to produce a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine. India imported its vaccines, and his eldest brother had died of hepatitis B infection at fifty. When SmithKline Beecham brought the first hepatitis B vaccine to India in the early 1990s, it was priced at Rs 1,400 a dose. Ella said he had proposed in 1994 to make one for a dollar. "None of the financial institutions in India were prepared to believe this," he said, and regulators, he later wrote, saw a field with no benchmark in the country.

The Ellas sold their personal assets in the United States and moved to Hyderabad in 1996 to start Bharat Biotech, with early support from family and fellow scientists in America. ICICI's venture capital arm had agreed to finance the project before they left; once they arrived, he said, "they dragged feet." A British venture fund's appraisal found the plan viable, and the Industrial Development Bank of India came in, holding a third of the shares by 2000. He used no contractors for the plant, he said, and watched every brick go up. Trial production began in October 1998, and the vaccine, Revac-B, was on the market in January 1999.

To lower the cost he developed his own purification method, which he called Himax. BioSpectrum later reported that the vaccine was first sold at Rs 800 a dose; by 2003, Ella said, UNICEF was buying it at 23 cents. "My only enemy is hepatitis-B," he told an interviewer in 2000.

quote.text: It was considered bad taste to speak of it, and ignorance of the value of different coins was a token of good breeding. Knowledge of numbers was indispensable in the mustering of forces as well, as in the distribution of benefices and fiefs; but the counting of money was left to meaner hands.
quote.locator: Chapter X, "The Education and Training of a Samurai"
quote.source_title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan, Project Gutenberg eBook #12096
quote.connection: Nitobe's samurai treated pricing as beneath a person of honour and left it to lesser hands. Ella, who wrote that money never motivated him, said the real challenge for a scientist was to envisage the price. The two views of money sit side by side here, unreconciled.

reflection: Ella did not decide alone, and he did not decide eagerly. He said plainly that he was uncomfortable. What moved him was a wife who could see where his science would matter and a mother who put a ceiling on what money could do for him.

You may be carrying a decision as if it belonged to you alone. Some of the clearest thinking about it may be sitting at your own table. And his mother's question, how much is enough, is worth answering early, on a rested day, before the numbers start arguing on your behalf.
invitation: Ask someone close to you, at home or at work, one plain question this week: what do they think your work is really for? Listen to the whole answer before you explain anything.

sources.title: Let's make India known for innovations

cross_checks.claim: Krishna Ella left the Medical University of South Carolina and returned to India in 1996 to found Bharat Biotech with his wife Suchitra.
His wife (and, in later accounts, his mother) urged the return.
The couple sold their personal assets in the US to fund the venture.
Ella proposed making a hepatitis B vaccine for about a dollar a dose when the prevailing price was far higher, and lenders and investors doubted it.
Revac-B went into trial production in October 1998 and was on the market in January 1999.
The vaccine was later supplied for about Rs 10 (23 cents) a dose.

research_notes: Kept, as instructed, to the 1996 return and the hepatitis B vaccine; the company's later products are not discussed. Who urged the return: in 2000 Ella credited his wife alone, and Business Today (2004) says he moved at her suggestion; from 2011 onwards (BioSpectrum, Wisconsin Alumni Association, and his own 2014 article) his mother is named too. The story gives the 2000 account first and then the later one. Years abroad: BioSpectrum (2003) quotes him saying 'After staying 15 years in the US', but he went abroad in 1986 and returned in 1996, so no figure is given. Launch: trial production October 1998 and product out January 1999 (Deccan Chronicle 2000; Ella 2014: rolled out January 1999); BioSpectrum (2003) gives commercial launch in 1998 with marketing from 1999, and the New Indian Express (1999) says launched in 1998. The story uses the 2000 interview's dates. Prices: SmithKline Beecham's early-1990s price is given as Rs 1,400 a dose (BioSpectrum 2003); the Wisconsin Alumni Association gives a going rate of $35 to $40; BioSpectrum (2011) gives Rs 1,012 ($22) per child before Bharat Biotech and says the vaccine was first sold at Rs 800 a dose. The story gives Rs 1,400 and Rs 800 with their sources, and does not say Revac-B was launched at a dollar: the dollar was Ella's 1994 proposal, and the 23 cents (Rs 10) figure is UNICEF's price by 2003 as he gave it. Funding: Ella's 2014 account names family and fellow US scientists; the New Indian Express (1999) lists US-based doctors among the promoters; the 2000 interview says IDBI held 33 per cent of the equity, so funding is set to mixed. The 2000 Deccan Chronicle and 2004 Business Today texts are cited from retyped copies in Bharat Biotech's own press archive, as the originals are not online; the claims taken from them are Ella's own words or are confirmed elsewhere (BioSpectrum 2003 on the sale of assets). Nitobe's passage describes the samurai's disdain for money in the education of a samurai; it is set beside Ella's view of pricing without resolving the difference.
